sentences.text: 2.  These bail applications are filed by the same person.
B.A. No.1310 of 2025 is filed under Section 483 of the BNSS and B.A. No.1590 of 2025 is filed under Section 482 of the BNSS.
3. These cases have a checkered history.
First, I will narrate the facts in B.A. No.1310 of 2025:
The petitioner is an accused in Crime No.1011 of 2024 of Irinjalakuda Police Station.
The petitioner originally filed Crl.M.C. No.174 of 2025 before this Court which resulted in Annexure-A2 order.
Thereafter the petitioner surrendered before the court.
But the bail application of the petitioner was not considered by the learned Magistrate.
Therefore the petitioner filed another Criminal Miscellaneous Case as Crl.M.C. B.A.Nos.1590 & 1310 of 2025 2025:KER:9912 No.584 of 2025.
In that Crl.M.C., this Court passed Annexure- A1 interim order directing the learned Magistrate to release the petitioner on interim bail.
Thereafter, the petitioner was released on bail based on Annexure-A1 order.
Subsequently, the learned Magistrate dismissed the bail application as evident by Annexure-A8.
According to the petitioner, he is in deemed custody and therefore the above bail application was filed under Section 483 of the BNSS.
When this bail application came up for consideration, the Public Prosecutor raised a preliminary point that the bail application is not maintainable.

Even though the counsel appearing for the petitioner submitted based on some Supreme Court decisions that the bail application is maintainable, even then this Court suggested the petitioner to file a bail application under Section 482 of the BNSS, and the petitioner filed B.A. No.1590 of 2025.
Today, these bail applications came up together.
4. Admittedly, the bail application filed by the petitioner was dismissed by the learned Magistrate as per Annexure-A8 order and he was directed to surrender within 15 days.

During that period, the petitioner filed these bail B.A.Nos.1590 & 1310 of 2025 2025:KER:9912 applications and this Court directed the Public Prosecutor to instruct the Investigating Officer not to arrest the petitioner.
Admittedly, the petitioner is not in custody.

Therefore, I am of the considered opinion that, B.A.
No.1310 of 2025 need not be considered.
5. B.A. No.1590 of 2025 is filed under Section 482 of the BNSS.
Petitioner is an accused in Crime No.1011 of 2024 of Irinjalakuda Police Station.
The above case is registered against the petitioner alleging offence punishable under Section 376(2)(n) of the IPC.

sentences.text: The prosecution case is that, after promising to marry the defacto complainant, the accused committed rape on her on 12.04.2024 in the bed room of the house of the petitioner situated on the western side of Irinjalakuda Koodalmanikyam temple and again on 12.05.2024 at 7 p.m., in the hall of the rental house of the defacto complainant situated on the southern side of the temple.
Hence it is alleged that the accused committed the above said offence.

7. Heard the learned counsel appearing for the petitioner, the learned counsel appearing for the defacto B.A.Nos.1590 & 1310 of 2025 2025:KER:9912 complainant and the learned Public Prosecutor.
8.

The counsel appearing for the defacto complainant seriously opposed the bail application and submitted that the petitioner cheated the defacto complainant, and this Court may not entertain this bail application.
9. This Court perused the First Information Statement of the defacto complainant.
Admittedly, the defacto complainant is aged 50 years and the petitioner is aged 51 years.
As per the First Information Statement, the defacto complainant divorced her husband and is now staying with her two children near Koodalmanikyam temple.
It is stated by the defacto complainant that she has known the petitioner from 2000 onwards.
According to the defacto complainant, the petitioner told her that he is going to divorce his wife and he will marry the defacto complainant.
It is also stated that on 05.05.2023, the defacto complainant was taken to the Kodungallur temple and a thali was tied.
Thereafter it is stated that, on two occasions, there was sexual relationship between the petitioner and the defacto complainant.
It is submitted that, subsequently, the petitioner did not contact the defacto B.A.Nos.1590 & 1310 of 2025 2025:KER:9912 complainant and hence the complaint was filed.
10. This Court considered the contentions of the petitioner, defacto complainant and the Public Prosecutor.

This Court also considered the dictum laid by the Apex Court in Mahesh Damu Khare v.
The State of Maharashtra & Anr. [2024 Live Law (SC) 921].

entities.text:
Mahesh Damu Khare v.
The State of Maharashtra & Anr. [2024 Live Law (SC) 921]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
The relevant portion is extracted hereunder:
"22.

In our view, if a man is accused of having sexual relationship by making a false promise of marriage and if he is to be held criminally liable, any such physical relationship must be traceable directly to the false promise made and not qualified by other circumstances or consideration.
A woman may have reasons to have physical relationship other than the promise of marriage made by the man, such as personal liking for the male partner without insisting upon formal marital ties.

Thus, in a situation where physical relationship is maintained for a prolonged period knowingly by the woman, it cannot be said with certainty that the said physical relationship was purely because of the alleged promise made by the appellant to marry her.

Thus,
unless it can be shown that the physical relationship was purely because of the promise of marriage, thereby having a direct nexus with the physical relationship without being influenced by any other consideration, it cannot be said that there was vitiation of consent under misconception of fact. "

Keeping in mind the above principle, this Court once again perused the First Information Statement.
I am of the considered opinion that, further custodial interrogation of the petitioner is not necessary.
Therefore, B.A. No.1590 of 2025 can be allowed after imposing stringent conditions.
11. Moreover, it is a well accepted principle that the bail is the rule and the jail is the exception.
The Hon'ble Supreme Court in Chidambaram.

P v. Directorate of Enforcement [2019 (16) SCALE 870],
after considering all the earlier judgments, observed that, the basic jurisprudence relating to bail remains the same inasmuch as the grant of bail is the rule and refusal is the exception so as to ensure that the accused has the opportunity of securing fair trial.

12. Recently the Apex Court in Siddharth v. State of Uttar Pradesh and Another [2021(5)KHC 353]
considered the point in detail.

entities.text: Siddharth v. State of Uttar Pradesh and Another [2021(5)KHC 353]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The relevant paragraph of the above judgment is extracted hereunder.
"12. We may note that personal liberty is an important aspect of our constitutional mandate.

The occasion to arrest an accused during investigation arises when custodial investigation becomes necessary or it is a heinous crime or where there is a possibility of influencing B.A.Nos.1590 & 1310 of 2025 2025:KER:9912 the witnesses or accused may abscond.
Merely because an arrest can be made because it is lawful does not mandate that arrest must be made.
A distinction must be made between the existence of the power to arrest and the justification for exercise of it.
(Joginder Kumar v. State of UP and Others (1994 KHC 189: (1994) 4 SCC 260: 1994 (1) KLT 919: 1994 (2) KLJ 97: AIR 1994 SC 1349: 1994 CriLJ 1981))

entities.text: Joginder Kumar v. State of UP and Others (1994 KHC 189: (1994) 4 SCC 260: 1994 (1) KLT 919: 1994 (2) KLJ 97: AIR 1994 SC 1349: 1994 CriLJ 1981)
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
If arrest is made routine,
it can cause incalculable harm to the reputation and self-esteem of a person.

If the Investigating Officer has no reason to believe that the accused will abscond or disobey summons and has, in fact, throughout cooperated with the investigation we fail to appreciate why there should be a compulsion on the officer to arrest the accused."

13. In Manish Sisodia v. Central Bureau of Investigation [2023 KHC 6961], the Apex Court observed that even if the allegation is one of grave economic offence, it is not a rule that bail should be denied in every case.

sentences.text: 14. Considering the dictum laid down in the above decision and considering the facts and circumstances of these cases, B.A. No.1310 of 2025 is closed and B.A. No.1590 of 2025 is allowed in the following manner:
1. The petitioner shall appear before the Investigating Officer within two B.A.Nos.1590 & 1310 of 2025 2025:KER:9912 weeks from today and shall undergo interrogation.

2. After interrogation, if the Investigating Officer propose to arrest the petitioner, he shall be released on bail on executing a bond for a sum of Rs.50,000/-
